piezas.explicacion: A small sounding-rocket engine, like the one of the WAC Corporal (1945). Simple and cheap, but it wastes a lot of propellant.
Small engine for upper stages. Low thrust, but it uses its propellant very efficiently (high Isp).
Powerful first-stage engine: it lifts a lot of weight, although it burns more propellant.
Designed to work outside the atmosphere: the most efficient engine, ideal for the last stage.
High-thrust engine for heavy rockets. Expensive, but big missions are impossible without it.
100 kg of propellant: enough for a short hop up and back down.
2 tonnes of propellant. Light: perfect for upper stages.
9 tonnes of propellant for a small first stage.
40 tonnes of propellant. It needs a very powerful engine to lift off.
A pointed nose that cuts through the air. There is room inside for a small experiment of up to 10 kg.
The nose of the rocket: it shields the satellite from the air during ascent. Takes up to 150 kg.
Takes satellites of up to 2 tonnes, but it is heavier and costs the rocket some Δv.
A satellite the size of a shoebox. Cheap, but only 4 components fit.
Twice the size of a 3U: 8 components fit and it lasts about 3 years.
Professional structure: 12 components and 10 years of life, but it weighs 60 kg.
Fixed to the satellite body. Cheap, but it only makes 3 W.
Unfolds like wings in orbit: more area facing the Sun, 8 W.
120 W for power-hungry instruments and antennas.
Stores energy for when the satellite passes through the Earth’s shadow and the panels get no light.
Ten times more energy to get through long shadows with everything switched on.
The satellite’s brain: nothing works without it.
Simple and cheap, but very slow (9.6 kbit/s): enough for status messages, not for photos.
2 Mbit/s: about 200 times faster than UHF. Lets you download images.
50 Mbit/s for missions that produce huge amounts of data. Uses a lot of power.
They spin to turn the satellite. Without them, cameras cannot point at their target.
Measures the Earth’s magnetic field. Light, low-power and it does not need pointing.
Photographs the surface. It produces 300 MB per day that you must be able to download.
Splits light into colors to reveal what things are made of: whether a crop is healthy, or which gases surround a distant star.
Highly detailed images: 4 GB per day. It needs a lot of power and a fast antenna.
Sees the infrared light our eyes miss, where cool stars like TRAPPIST-1 shine brightest. A tiny fridge keeps its detector below −150 °C, so it uses a lot of power.
A smaller copy of Parker Solar Probe's shield: carbon foam between two carbon plates, painted white. Its front glows at about 1,400 °C while the probe behind it stays near 30 °C.

orbitas.explicacion: Close to Earth: the cheapest orbit to reach and photos come out sharp, but the remaining air slows the satellite down and it falls within about 2 years. It spends little time over each ground antenna.
Passes over the poles and over every place at the same solar time, so the lighting is the same in every photo. Higher up: it lasts for decades and spends more time over polar antennas.
It goes around once in the time the Earth takes to spin: it seems to stand still in the sky, so a fixed antenna always sees it. Getting there costs a huge amount of Δv.

orbitas.nombre: Lunar orbit (100 km above the Moon)
orbitas.explicacion: The rocket first reaches low orbit, then fires again towards the Moon (a 3-day trip) and brakes to be captured. The Moon’s lumpy gravity slowly pulls low orbits down, and the giant antennas of NASA’s Deep Space Network only listen to you a few hours a day.

orbitas.nombre: Sun–Earth L2 (1.5 million km, where Webb orbits)
orbitas.explicacion: 1.5 million km from Earth, on the side away from the Sun. A telescope here circles the L2 point every 6 months, never enters a shadow and can keep the heat of the Sun and Earth behind it. Small thruster burns keep it in place, so its propellant sets how long it lasts.

orbitas.nombre: Close solar orbit (6 million km from the Sun)
orbitas.explicacion: To fall towards the Sun you must cancel most of the 107,000 km/h at which Earth carries you around it: 55 times the energy of a trip to Mars. Parker Solar Probe also needed seven Venus flybys. Up close, only a heat shield keeps the probe alive, and radio contact is lost for days.

preguntas.pregunta: About how much did the James Webb Space Telescope cost NASA?
preguntas.explicacion: GAO put Webb at $9.7 billion: development plus 5 years of operations. Its cost nearly doubled after 2009 as problems piled up.

preguntas.pregunta: What did Project Apollo (1960–1973) cost the US at the time?
preguntas.explicacion: $25.8 billion in the money of the time, about $300 billion in today's dollars. It landed astronauts on the Moon six times.

preguntas.pregunta: Roughly what does SpaceX charge for one whole Falcon 9 launch?
preguntas.explicacion: SpaceX advertised $62 million in 2018 and about $70 million in recent years. Landing and reusing the first stage helps keep it low.

preguntas.pregunta: The Shuttle cost ~$54,500 per kg to low orbit. What did Falcon 9 advertise in 2018?
preguntas.explicacion: $62 million for 22,800 kg: about $2,720 per kg, 20 times cheaper. After decades of flat prices, commercial rockets cut launch costs (NASA Ames).

preguntas.pregunta: What share of all US federal spending went to NASA in 2025?
preguntas.explicacion: About 0.35%: roughly a third of a cent of every dollar the US government spends. NASA's share peaked during Apollo in the 1960s.

preguntas.pregunta: Roughly how big was NASA's budget in 2025?
preguntas.explicacion: $24.8 billion in 2025 and $24.4 billion in 2026. It pays for science missions, Artemis, the space station, aeronautics and more.

preguntas.pregunta: Who decides how much money NASA gets each year?
preguntas.explicacion: The President proposes a budget, but Congress passes the appropriations laws that actually fund NASA with taxpayers' money.

preguntas.pregunta: By 2013, about how much had the US spent on the International Space Station?
preguntas.explicacion: NASA's Inspector General counted almost $75 billion: building it plus 37 Shuttle flights. Running it costs NASA about $3 billion a year.

preguntas.pregunta: What does NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative give schools and nonprofits?
preguntas.explicacion: Teams fund and build their own CubeSat; NASA finds it a spot on a rocket. Over 150 student and nonprofit CubeSats have flown this way.

preguntas.pregunta: Mars Pathfinder (1997) was 'faster, better, cheaper'. What did the whole mission cost?
preguntas.explicacion: About $265 million with launch and operations: $150 million for the lander and about $25 million for Sojourner, the first rover on Mars.

preguntas.pregunta: Roughly what did designing and building the Parker Solar Probe cost?
preguntas.explicacion: Around $1.3 billion. In 2007 NASA had asked for a Sun mission under $750 million: the hard engineering made it grow.

preguntas.pregunta: NASA's Inspector General estimated one SLS/Orion Moon launch (Artemis I–IV) costs?
preguntas.explicacion: $4.1 billion per launch just to build and fly it, without the years of development. The Inspector General called that unsustainable.

preguntas.pregunta: What did the Ingenuity Mars helicopter cost to build and fly?
preguntas.explicacion: About $80 million to build and $5 million to operate. Planned for 5 flights, it made 72: a small technology demo that paid off.

preguntas.pregunta: GAO's lesson from Webb's overruns: what must big space projects plan for?
preguntas.explicacion: Webb's reserves for surprises were too small. Covering its overruns forced NASA to take money from other science missions and delay them.

preguntas.pregunta: How much erasable (RAM) memory did the Apollo Guidance Computer have?
preguntas.explicacion: Just 2K words of erasable memory plus 36K words of fixed 'core rope' memory, and it still guided astronauts to the Moon and back.

preguntas.pregunta: During Apollo 11's Moon landing, what did the '1202' alarm mean?
preguntas.explicacion: Executive overflow: too many jobs at once. The software restarted, kept the vital landing tasks, dropped the rest, and the landing went on.

preguntas.pregunta: Why was NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter lost in 1999?
preguntas.explicacion: Ground software gave thruster data in pound-seconds; navigation expected newton-seconds. The orbiter arrived far too low and was lost at Mars.

preguntas.pregunta: What destroyed the Ariane 5 rocket on its first flight in 1996?
opciones: A number too big for 16 bits
preguntas.explicacion: Reused Ariane 4 code squeezed a 64-bit velocity value into a 16-bit integer. It overflowed, both guidance computers shut down and the rocket broke up.

preguntas.pregunta: In 2024, how did NASA fix Voyager 1's computer, 24 billion km away?
opciones: Moved code around a dead chip
Switched it off for a year
preguntas.explicacion: A failed memory chip garbled its data. Engineers split the code into pieces, stored them elsewhere in memory and sent the patch by radio.

preguntas.pregunta: Perseverance's radiation-hardened RAD750 processor runs at up to about what speed?
preguntas.explicacion: Slow next to a phone, but built so space radiation doesn't crash it. The rover carries two identical computers, so there's always a spare 'brain'.

preguntas.pregunta: What kind of processor flew the Ingenuity helicopter on Mars?
preguntas.explicacion: A Qualcomm Snapdragon 801 phone chip running Linux. Faster than the rover's computer but not radiation-hardened: a risk accepted for a short demo.

preguntas.pregunta: How did the Space Shuttle's computers catch one that went wrong?
preguntas.explicacion: Four computers ran the same software and compared results; one that disagreed was voted out. A fifth ran separately written backup software.

preguntas.pregunta: What usually causes random 'bit flips' in a spacecraft's memory?
preguntas.explicacion: A cosmic ray or proton can leave enough charge in a chip to turn a 0 into a 1. Error-correcting memory and voting computers catch it.

preguntas.pregunta: Why does NASA's Deep Space Network have sites in California, Spain and Australia?
opciones: To see probes as Earth spins
preguntas.explicacion: Spread around the globe, one site picks up a spacecraft as another loses it below the horizon. Each site has a giant 70 m dish.

preguntas.pregunta: Why can't Perseverance be driven live with a joystick from Earth?
preguntas.explicacion: Commands take 3 to 22 minutes to arrive, so drivers send a whole day's plan at once and the rover's own software steers around hazards.

preguntas.pregunta: How much science data can the Webb telescope send to Earth per day?
preguntas.explicacion: Two 4-hour Deep Space Network contacts a day, each carrying at least 28.6 GB. Its recorder holds only about 65 GB, so it must empty daily.

preguntas.pregunta: What caused Hubble's blurry images after its 1990 launch?
preguntas.explicacion: Not software: a test tool set up 1.3 mm off let the mirror be polished too flat at the edge. Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993.

preguntas.pregunta: What did Curiosity receive a few days after landing on Mars in 2012?
preguntas.explicacion: A 'brain transplant': its landing software was replaced with driving and robotic-arm software, sent by radio. Rovers are built to be reprogrammed.

estrellas.descripcion: The closest star to the Sun. It has a planet, Proxima b, in the zone where liquid water could exist.
estrellas.reto: A sharp camera to spot a small planet next to its star.

estrellas.descripcion: A tiny, cool star with seven Earth-sized planets. The James Webb telescope is studying their atmospheres.
estrellas.reto: An infrared instrument: the star is cool and shines mostly in infrared.

estrellas.descripcion: A giant star in Orion, so big it would swallow Jupiter's orbit. One day it will explode as a supernova.
estrellas.reto: A spectrometer to read the light of a star that keeps changing.

estrellas.descripcion: Our own star. In 2024 the Parker Solar Probe flew 6 million km from its surface, faster than any machine before.
estrellas.reto: A heat shield and a huge amount of Δv to fall towards the Sun.

destinos.hito: Climb at least 10 km and splash down in the ocean.
destinos.referenciaReal: In 1945 the WAC Corporal, a small US sounding rocket, climbed about 70 km before falling back.

destinos.hito: Cross the Kármán line, 100 km up, where space begins.
destinos.referenciaReal: In 1946 a V-2 rocket launched from White Sands took the first photos of the Earth from space, 105 km up.

destinos.hito: Put a working satellite into low Earth orbit.
destinos.referenciaReal: Explorer 1 (1958), the first US satellite, discovered the Van Allen radiation belts around the Earth.

destinos.hito: Put a working satellite into geostationary orbit.
destinos.referenciaReal: Syncom 3 (1964) was the first geostationary satellite: it broadcast the Tokyo Olympics across the Pacific.

destinos.hito: Put a probe into orbit around the Moon.
destinos.referenciaReal: NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has been mapping the Moon from orbit since 2009.

destinos.hito: Put a probe into orbit around Mars.
destinos.referenciaReal: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (2005) photographs Mars in enough detail to see the rovers on its surface.

destinos.hito: Find a habitable planet with a space telescope.
destinos.referenciaReal: NASA’s planned Habitable Worlds Observatory will search for Earth-like planets around other stars.

misiones.descripcion: You only have parts for one small rocket. Make it climb at least 10 km and let it fall safely into the ocean.
Space begins at the Kármán line, 100 km above the sea. Build a rocket that crosses it.
Going up and falling back is not enough: put a working CubeSat into low Earth orbit, where it keeps circling the planet.
Put a working satellite into geostationary orbit, 35,786 km up, where it seems to stand still in the sky.
Send a probe into orbit around the Moon and map its surface with a camera. It is the first step away from the Earth.
Measure the magnetic field that protects the Earth from the solar wind for at least 10 months.
Farmers need daily images to spot pests and droughts. Deliver at least 250 MB of images per day for a year.
Watch the storms over a whole continent without losing sight of them for 5 years. It takes a large satellite far from Earth.
The Government no longer pays you for missions. Prove you can put a satellite into orbit to win back its trust.
